entities.name: Li Ling
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Li Ling (李陵, courtesy name Shaoqing) was a prominent military general of the Western Han dynasty whose career, marked by a disastrous frontier campaign and subsequent defection to the Xiongnu confederacy in 99 BCE, profoundly impacted the political landscape and intellectual discourse of Emperor Wu's reign. His story became a crucible for testing the Han court's values of loyalty, military prowess, and the treatment of defeated commanders, notably triggering the infamous castration of historian Sima Qian for his defense. Li Ling's fate encapsulates the perilous nature of Han-Xiongnu relations and the harsh expectations placed upon aristocratic military families in securing the empire's northern borders, making him a poignant figure in Chinese historiography.

Born into a distinguished military family, Li Ling was the grandson of the renowned "Flying General" Li Guang. He rose through the ranks, gaining a reputation for his skill in cavalry and archery. His defining moment came in 99 BCE when, leading a force of 5,000 infantry, he was dispatched on an expedition against the Xiongnu in the Tian Shan mountains, intended as a diversion for General Li Guangli's larger campaign. Despite inflicting heavy casualties on the numerically superior Xiongnu forces, Li Ling's detachment was eventually overwhelmed after running out of arrows and supplies, leading to his surrender to the Xiongnu Chanyu. This defeat, though fiercely fought, was perceived as a profound disgrace by Emperor Wu and much of the Han court.
